Step 1: Document Your Work

For this workshop, I decided to document the complete analysis in a
single R Markdown file rather than creating a separate document for each
analysis step.

The R Markdown file used for this project is:

``` text
Workshop_4_BBD_analysis.Rmd
```

The document title is:

``` text
Workshop 4: Black Band Disease Metagenome Analysis
```

This file contains the complete workflow, including:

-   metagenome assembly using Flye;
-   genome binning using MetaBAT2;
-   bin quality assessment using CheckM;
-   functional analysis;
-   results and interpretation.

Using one R Markdown document keeps the complete workflow in one place
and makes it easier to follow the analysis from beginning to end.

Step 2 \# Step 2: Assembly with Flye

The purpose of this step was to assemble Oxford Nanopore reads from the
black band disease microbial community into contigs.

## Create the Flye Directory

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
cd ~/marine-genomics
mkdir flye
cd flye
```

## Link the Sequencing Data

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
ln -s /pvol/data/metagenome_assembly/bbd_0.1.fastq.gz .
```

## Create the SLURM Script

A shell script called `run_flye_bbd.sh` was created inside the `flye`
directory.

``` bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --time=720
#SBATCH --ntasks=12 --mem=10gb

echo "Starting flye bbd in $(pwd) at $(date)"

flye --nano-hq ../flye/bbd_0.1.fastq.gz --threads 12 --out-dir bbd --meta

echo "Finished flye bbd in $(pwd) at $(date)"
```

## Submit the Job

``` bash
sbatch run_flye_bbd.sh
```

## Monitor the Job

``` bash
squeue -u $USER
```

Job status:

``` text
PD = Pending
R  = Running
```

The SLURM output file can be checked using:

``` bash
tail -f slurm-XXX.out
```

My slurm number was 591 \## GitHub Files

Only the R Markdown file and shell script should be added to GitHub.

git add Workshop_4_BBD_analysis.Rmd git add flye/run_flye_bbd.sh git
commit -m "Add Flye assembly workflow" git push

```         

Large sequencing and Flye output files should not be uploaded to GitHub.

# Step 3: Binning with MetaBAT2

After the Flye assembly was completed, the assembled contigs were grouped into genome bins using MetaBAT2.

## Create the MetaBAT Directory

```bash
cd ~/marine-genomics
mkdir metabat
cd metabat
```

## Extract Depth Information

Depth information was extracted from the Flye assembly output:

``` bash
cat ../flye/bbd/assembly_info.txt  | grep -v '#' | awk '{OFS="\t";print $1,$3}' > depths_bbd.txt
```

The output file can be checked using:

``` bash
head depths_bbd.txt
```

## Reorder the Contigs

The contigs were reordered so that the FASTA file matched the order of
the depth file:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
cat depths_bbd.txt | awk '{print $1}' | xargs samtools faidx ../flye/bbd/assembly.fasta > assembly_bbd_ordered.fasta
```

The reordered assembly can be checked using:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
ls -lh assembly_bbd_ordered.fasta
```

## Run MetaBAT2

``` bash
metabat2 -i assembly_bbd_ordered.fasta -a depths_bbd.txt --cvExt -o bins_bbd/metabat --seed 5
```

# Step 4: Check Bin Quality with CheckM

CheckM was used to assess the quality of the bins produced by MetaBAT2.

## Create the CheckM Directory

``` bash
cd ~/marine-genomics
mkdir checkm
cd checkm
```

## Find the Largest Contig

``` bash
cat ../flye/bbd/assembly.fasta | bioawk -c fastx '{print length($seq),$name}' | sort -n
```

The largest contig was:

``` text
4706700 contig_133
```

## Prepare the Bins

```         
mkdir bins_bbd
cp ../metabat/bins_bbd/*.fa bins_bbd/
```

The largest contig was added manually:

```         
samtools faidx ../flye/bbd/assembly.fasta contig_133 \
  > bins_bbd/contig_133.fa
```

A script called `run_checkm_bbd.sh` was created:

```         
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --time=60
#SBATCH --ntasks=6
#SBATCH --mem=10gb

echo "Starting checkm in $(pwd) at $(date)"

shopt -s expand_aliases
alias checkm='apptainer run -B /pvol/:/pvol /pvol/data/sif/checkm.sif checkm'

checkm lineage_wf bins_bbd out \
  -t 4 \
  -x fa \
  -f checkm_results_bbd.txt

echo "Finished checkm in $(pwd) at $(date)"
```

## Submit the Job

```         
sbatch run_checkm_bbd.sh
```

# Step 5: Select Bins Based on CheckM Results

The CheckM results were used to select the most complete genome bins for
further functional analysis.

## View the CheckM Results

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
cd ~/marine-genomics/checkm
head checkm_results_bbd.txt
```

More results were viewed using:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
head -n 20 checkm_results_bbd.txt
```

## Select Bins with Completeness Greater Than 15%

The following command selected bins with completeness greater than 15%:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
cat checkm_results_bbd.txt | awk '$13 > 15'
```

Only the bin IDs were extracted using:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
cat checkm_results_bbd.txt | awk '$13 > 15 {print $1}'
```

The selected bin IDs were saved to a new file:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
cat checkm_results_bbd.txt \
  | awk '$13 > 15 {print $1}' \
  > bbd_topbins.txt
```

The file was checked using:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
cat bbd_topbins.txt
```

## Results

A total of 12 bins had completeness greater than 15%:

``` text
contig_133
metabat.28
metabat.33
metabat.35
metabat.68
metabat.11
metabat.42
metabat.32
metabat.58
metabat.26
metabat.2
metabat.34
```

The number of selected bins was confirmed using:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
wc -l bbd_topbins.txt
```

Expected output:

``` text
12 bbd_topbins.txt
```

These bins were selected because they were more complete than the
remaining bins and were more likely to contain useful information about

# Step 7: Gene Annotation with Prokka

Prokka was used to identify genes and assign possible functions to genes
within the selected genome bins.

## Create the Prokka Directory

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
cd ~/marine-genomics
mkdir prokka
cd prokka
```

## Test Prokka on One Bin

The first bin in the selected-bin list was checked using:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
head -n 1 ../checkm/bbd_topbins.txt
```

The first bin was:

``` text
contig_133
```

Prokka was tested on this bin:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
bin=metabat.5
prokka --outdir $bin --prefix $bin  ../metabat/bins_bbd/${bin}.fa
```

The output files were checked using:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
ls metabat.5
```

## Run Prokka on All Selected Bins

A SLURM script called `run_prokka.sh` was created inside the `prokka`
directory.

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --time=60
#SBATCH --ntasks=2 --mem=2gb

echo "Starting prokka in $(pwd) at $(date)"

shopt -s expand_aliases
alias prokka='apptainer run -B /pvol/:/pvol /pvol/data/sif/prokka.sif prokka'

while read bin;do 
  prokka --outdir $bin --prefix $bin "../metabat/bins_bbd/${bin}.fa";
done < ../checkm/bbd_topbins.txt

echo "Finished prokka in $(pwd) at $(date)"
```

## Submit the Prokka Job

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
sbatch run_prokka.sh
```

Step 8

# Step 8: Infer Metabolic Pathways with MinPath

MinPath was used to infer metabolic pathways from the genes annotated by
Prokka.

The aim was to identify possible biological functions within the black
band disease microbial community, including processes such as
photosynthesis and sulfate reduction.

## Create the MinPath Directory

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
cd ~/marine-genomics
mkdir minpath
cd minpath
```

## Inspect a Prokka Annotation File

The Prokka `.tsv` file for one bin was viewed using:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
head ../prokka/metabat.5/metabat.5.tsv
```

The Prokka output contained gene IDs, gene lengths, predicted gene
names, EC numbers, COG identifiers, and protein functions. Most of the
first genes were annotated as hypothetical proteins, meaning their
functions could not be confidently identified. One gene, `bcrA`, was
identified as a bacitracin transport ATP-binding protein.

## Prepare MinPath Input

MinPath requires the gene ID and EC number.

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
head ../prokka/metabat.5/metabat.5.tsv | awk -F '\t' '{print $1,$5}'
```

The option `-F '\t'` tells `awk` that the file is tab-separated.

Next, only genes with an EC number were selected:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
head ../prokka/metabat.5/metabat.5.tsv | awk -F '\t' '$5{print $1,$5}'
```

The output was then formatted as tab-separated data and the header was
removed:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
head ../prokka/metabat.5/metabat.5.tsv | awk -F '\t' '$5{OFS="\t";print $1,$5}' | grep -v '^locus'
```

Because `head` only processes the first 10 lines, `cat` was used to
process the complete file:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
cat ../prokka/metabat.5/metabat.5.tsv | awk -F '\t' '$5{OFS="\t";print $1,$5}' | grep -v '^locus'
```

The final MinPath input was saved as:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
cat ../prokka/metabat.5/metabat.5.tsv | awk -F '\t' '$5{OFS="\t";print $1,$5}' | grep -v '^locus' > metabat.5.ec
```

The file can be checked using:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
head metabat.5.ec
```

## Run MinPath

MinPath was run using:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
minpath -ec metabat.5.ec -report metabat.5.ec.report -details metabat.5.ec.details
```

The first lines of the pathway report were viewed using:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
head metabat.5.ec.report
```

An example line from the MinPath report is:

``` text
path PWY-7321 any n/a naive 1 minpath 0 fam0 4 fam-found 2 name ecdysteroid metabolism (arthropods)
```

The important parts are:

-   `PWY-7321` is the pathway identifier in the MetaCyc database.
-   `fam0 4` means that the pathway contains four gene families.
-   `fam-found 2` means that two of those gene families were detected in
    this genome bin.
-   `name ecdysteroid metabolism (arthropods)` is the pathway name.

This means that only part of the pathway was detected. Therefore, the
pathway may be present, but the evidence is incomplete and should be
interpreted carefully.

## Run MinPath for All Selected Bins

After Prokka finished, MinPath input files were prepared for all
selected bins.

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
while read bin;do 
  cat ../prokka/$bin/${bin}.tsv | awk -F '\t' '$5{printf("%s\t%s\n", $1,$5)}' | grep -v '^locus' > ${bin}.ec 
done < ../checkm/bbd_topbins.txt
```

This created one `.ec` file for each selected bin.

MinPath was then run for all bins:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
while read bin;do 
  minpath -ec ${bin}.ec -report ${bin}.ec.report -details ${bin}.ec.details
done < ../checkm/bbd_topbins.txt
```

## Search for Photosynthesis Pathways

The pathway `PWY-101` represents photosynthesis light reactions,
including components of Photosystem I and Photosystem II.

The pathway was searched across all MinPath reports using:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
grep 'PWY-101' *.ec.report
```

The results were:

``` text
contig_133      minpath 0   fam0 4   fam-found 1
metabat.28      minpath 1   fam0 4   fam-found 4
metabat.42      minpath 1   fam0 4   fam-found 1
metabat.58      minpath 0   fam0 4   fam-found 1
metabat.5       minpath 1   fam0 4   fam-found 1
```

`metabat.28` provided the strongest evidence for photosynthesis because
all four gene families associated with the pathway were detected.

The other bins contained only one of the four gene families. Therefore,
their evidence for a complete photosynthesis light-reaction pathway was
weak.

This result is consistent with the GTDB/CheckM classification of
`metabat.28` as Cyanobacteria, which are expected to be the main
photosynthetic members of the black band disease community.

Although `metabat.42` and `metabat.5` had `minpath 1`, only one gene
family was detected in each bin. These pathway predictions should
therefore be interpreted cautiously.

### Question 4.1

How many bins contain at least one gene from this pathway? Which bin has
all of the genes (ie a complete pathway)?

Five bins contained at least one gene family from the photosynthesis
light-reaction pathway `PWY-101`:

``` text
contig_133
metabat.28
metabat.42
metabat.58
metabat.5
```

Only `metabat.28` contained all four gene families required for the
pathway:

5 bins contained at least one gene from PWY-101, and metabat.28
contained the complete pathway. It was classified as Cyanobacteria,
family Desertifilaceae, genus Roseofilum.

### Cross-reference `PWY-5360` with GTDB-Tk

The taxonomy of `metabat.35` was checked using:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
grep -P '^metabat\.35\t' \
  ../gtdbtk/out/gtdbtk.bac120.summary.tsv
```

The result classified `metabat.35` as:

``` text
Phylum: Campylobacterota
Class: Campylobacteria
Order: Campylobacterales
Family: Arcobacteraceae
Genus: Halarcobacter
```

### Question 4.2

How many bins contain the pathway PWY-5360? What family (in a taxonomic
sense) do these bins belong to?

One bin contained the pathway `PWY-5360`: `metabat.35`. This bin
belonged to the family **Arcobacteraceae**.
